newsitem.title: USA: Human remains found in Colorado wreck of warplane.
newsitem.headline: Human remains found in Colorado wreck of warplane.

text.p: Searchers on Friday found what could be the remains of the missing pilot of an A-10 attack aircraft that crashed on a Rocky Mountain peak after it disappeared on April 2 loaded with bombs.
Human remains were recovered from the snow-covered wreckage of the plane and authorities were trying to determine if they were the pilot's remains.
"What we found was fragmentary human remains," Air Force Major General Nels Running told reporters at search headquarters in Eagle, Colorado.

The A-10 warplane disappeared during a routine training mission on April 2 and Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles away (1,360 km) from a training exercise in Arizona.
The plane apparently slammed into the side of the mountain but was not found until last Sunday.

"We are positive they are human remains, we are not positive whose human remains they are," Running said, adding that investigators planned to perform DNA tests to determine if they belonged to Button.
Running declined to specify what remains were found by the rescue team, but he said results from identification tests should be known within 72 hours.
They were recovered on Friday after weather conditions allowed the Air Force to launch its first intensive search for the missing pilot.

Air Force spokesman Capt. Mike Richmond earlier said a three-man para-rescue team was lowered from a MH-53 heavy-lift helicopter to the crash site 12,500 feet (3,800 metres) up New York Mountain while a two-man team was dropped off at a base camp below the wreckage.

One of the priorities of the para-rescue team was to determine if Button was on the plane when it crashed into the side of New York Mountain in the remote range southeast of the Vail ski resort, Air Force officials said.
Running told reporters on Thursday the search would continue until Button was found. "We don't close the books until we have conclusion," he said.
The plane wreckage was spotted on Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain.
The Air Force confirmed on Wednesday that it was the missing A-10 after a para-rescuer at the end of a helicopter rope had plucked two small pieces of the wreckage off the mountain.

Button, whose plane was carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs, broke formation after leaving the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona, headed for the Barry M. Goldwater Bombing Range in Arizona.
